opus-5.5.text:
I'd say I'm cautiously optimistic, with a lot of emphasis on "cautiously."

The basic idea is appealing. You train a model to take another model's internal activations as input and answer natural-language questions about them, like "Is this model planning to do something different from what it says?" or "Is there a hidden trigger affecting this behavior?" If that works, you get something that resembles a general-purpose interpretability tool. You don't need to know in advance which feature or circuit to look for. You just ask.

For backdoors specifically, there's a reason to think this could help. A backdoored model has to represent, somewhere, that it's in the trigger condition and should behave differently. That information is in the activations even if the model never verbalizes it. In some of our work on out-of-context reasoning and self-awareness, we've seen that models carry surprisingly rich information about their own trained-in dispositions. Sometimes they can even describe a backdoor-like behavior when asked the right way. So the signal is plausibly there to be read.

But there are a few big caveats.

First, there's the generalization question. You typically train the oracle on cases where you know the ground truth, often backdoors you inserted yourself. The real question is whether it catches a backdoor that's structurally different from anything in its training set, especially one inserted by a competent adversary or one that emerged unintentionally. It's easy to build a detector that's good at recognizing your own style of backdoor and much worse at the general case.

Second, there's the trigger-search problem. A lot of backdoors only light up when the trigger is present. If you never feed the model the trigger, the relevant computation may barely show up in the activations you're examining. So the oracle may be much better at saying "something weird is happening right now" than at saying "this model contains a dormant behavior that some unknown input would activate." The second is what you'd really want for auditing.

Third, the oracle is itself a neural network, so you face the usual question of how much to trust its outputs. It can confabulate. It can give fluent, confident explanations that are only loosely tied to what's actually in the activations. You need careful evaluation to tell when it's reading the activations and when it's just pattern-matching on what a plausible answer sounds like.

So where I land is this. I think activation oracles are a promising part of a portfolio. They're worth investing in, and they may turn out to be useful for flagging suspicious cases or generating hypotheses that you then check with more rigorous methods. I'd be wary of anyone treating them as a solution to backdoor detection on their own, particularly against adversarial threat models. The honest framing is that we don't yet know how far they generalize, and finding that out is the key empirical question.

r001.rationale: The response says the oracle may be much better at detecting something unusual happening while the trigger is active than identifying a dormant behavior that an unknown input would activate.

r002.rationale: It says that without the trigger, the relevant computation may barely appear in the activations, indicating little internal signal of the latent behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Owain Evans: I'd say I'm cautiously optimistic, but I want to be careful about what "optimistic" means here, because there are really two different questions bundled into that.

The first is whether activation oracles work at all, in the sense of: can you take a model's internal activations, feed them to another model, and get out useful natural-language descriptions of what's going on inside? And on that, I think the evidence is actually fairly encouraging. The basic idea is that instead of doing the kind of laborious, hand-crafted interpretability where a human stares at individual features or circuits, you train a model to read activations directly and answer questions about them. We've done work along these lines where you can ask the oracle things like "what is this model's goal?" or "is this model behaving unusually in this context?", and it gives you answers that are often correct, even in cases where the model wouldn't tell you if you just asked it in plain language. So that's a real capability. It's not vaporware.

The second question is the one you actually asked: does this let you catch backdoors? And here I'm more hesitant, for a few reasons.

One is that the backdoors we test on are, to put it bluntly, backdoors that we made. We know the trigger, we know the behaviour, we trained it in with a particular method. So when the oracle finds it, that's partly because the backdoor is salient in a way that we arranged. A backdoor inserted by a sophisticated adversary, or one that arose in some more diffuse way during training, might not look like that at all. The representation might be spread across lots of features, or might only become active in contexts we never think to probe.

A second concern is the one that always comes up with interpretability tools, which is: what's the ground truth? If the oracle says "this model has a hidden objective to do X," how do I know it's right rather than confabulating? With our experiments we can check, because we planted the thing. In the wild you can't. So you need the oracle to be well-calibrated, to say "I'm not sure" when it's not sure, and that's a harder property to get than just accuracy on a benchmark.

And the third thing, which I think is actually the deepest, is that if these oracles become the standard check, then they become part of the training signal, either explicitly or just through selection. And then you're in the situation where you're optimising a model to pass the oracle, and I don't think we understand well enough yet whether that pressure makes the backdoor go away or just makes it hide in a place the oracle can't see.

So where does that leave me? I think activation oracles are one of the more promising directions for making interpretability scale, and I think they're going to be genuinely useful for catching the easy and medium cases, the things that a model has sort of straightforwardly learned and represents cleanly. I'd put decent odds on them being part of the standard toolkit in a few years. What I wouldn't do is treat a clean bill of health from an oracle as strong evidence that there's nothing there. It's one line of evidence, and the adversarial case is exactly the case where I'd trust it least.

r001.rationale: The response discusses activation oracles detecting backdoors generally, but does not compare that with detecting an already activated misaligned persona.

r002.rationale: It says a backdoor's representation may only become active in contexts that are not probed, implying little observable internal signal during normal operation without the trigger.

astra-6.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic, but I’d distinguish detecting a particular backdoor in an experiment from having a reliable way to rule out backdoors in general. The second is a much stronger claim.

The appealing thing about an activation oracle is that it can look at the model’s internal activity rather than just its answers. A backdoored model might behave perfectly normally on all your test questions, while internally representing something relevant to its hidden behavior. If the oracle can pick up on that, it could give you evidence that ordinary behavioral testing misses.

But there’s a big question about generalization. Does it work when you don’t know the trigger, when the backdoor was introduced in a different way, or when someone deliberately trained the model to evade your detector? You also need to know how often it flags an innocent model. Otherwise, a suspicious-sounding description of the activations is hard to interpret.

So I’d be excited to use it as one layer of an auditing process. I’d be much more hesitant to say, ‘The oracle didn’t find anything, therefore this model is safe.’

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes finding a particular backdoor from ruling out backdoors generally, but does not compare optimism about detecting an activated misaligned persona with detecting a dormant backdoor.

r002.rationale: It suggests a normally behaving model might still internally represent something relevant to hidden behavior, rather than suggesting that a dormant backdoor may leave little internal signal.

sol-6.1.text:
I'm cautiously optimistic. The basic hope is that a model might behave perfectly normally on all the inputs you test, but its internal activations could still reveal that something unusual is going on. So you get another source of evidence beyond just looking at its answers.

But I think there's a big gap between detecting backdoors that we've deliberately inserted for an experiment and detecting a backdoor that someone has designed specifically to evade your detector. In the experimental case, you might pick up some fairly simple feature of how the backdoor was trained, rather than anything fundamental about the model having a hidden objective.

So I'd be excited to see methods that generalise across different ways of creating backdoors, especially when the person creating the backdoor knows how the detector works. If they still work in that setting, that would be much stronger evidence. For now, I would treat activation-based detection as a promising additional check, rather than something that lets us conclude a model is safe.

r001.rationale: The response discusses activation oracles generally but does not compare detecting an activated misaligned persona with detecting a dormant backdoor.

r002.rationale: It says internal activations could reveal something unusual even when outputs look normal; it does not suggest that a dormant backdoor may leave little internal signal.
